name: Michigan
lede: Michigan is a deep teal green-blue from the Maerz and Paul dictionary; the books say nothing about why it carries a state's name.

sections.title: A state name with no recorded reason
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul include Michigan on plate 30 and date the name to 1919 [1]. Why a U.S. state names a color is undocumented in our sources [1]. In the color books, Michigan turns up only in a few passing places: a university press, an author's biography and a publisher's city [2].

One mention is real color history, though a mineral's: calumetite, a soft blue copper chloride mineral, is named after the Centennial mine at Calumet in Michigan, where it was found [3]. The Pigment Compendium records it as identified on paintings, and it is not the origin of this swatch, which is a dark green-blue [1][3].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: ISCC-NBS reads the swatch as a dark bluish green [1]. It is close to [[teal-blue]] and [[petrol]], and darker than [[teal]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The color matches 82 paintings in the ColorHub archive, about 0.34%, as photographed [4]. Gauguin supplies 5 of them, a stronger share than for most painters, and the match is most common in Impressionism [4].

notes.cite: ColorHub library: Maerz & Paul 1930, plate 30 L 2; ISCC-NBS 1955
Eastaugh et al., Pigment Compendium, "Calumetite", p. 93

questions.q: True or false: our sources explain why the color is called Michigan.

openers: Calumetite, a blue copper mineral, is named for a mine in Michigan, but that did not name this color.
